raw_text:
### Introduction and Pathophysiology
Cardiac amyloidosis (CA) represents a major clinical challenge and is increasingly recognized as a key cause of heart failure, restrictive cardiomyopathy, and mortality [1]. The disease is characterized by the extracellular deposition of misfolded protein fibrils within the myocardial interstitium, leading to progressive ventricular wall thickening, diastolic stiffness, and clinical heart failure [2]. Although more than 30 proteins can form systemic amyloid fibrils, the vast majority of clinically significant cardiac cases are driven by two precursor proteins: monoclonal immunoglobulin light chains or transthyretin [3,4].

The first primary subtype, light-chain cardiac amyloidosis (AL-CA), is a hematologic disorder stemming from a clonal plasma cell dyscrasia [5]. The clone overproduces unstable immunoglobulin light chains, which undergo misfolding, aggregate into amyloid fibrils, and exert direct proteotoxic effects on cardiomyocytes [5]. The second major subtype, transthyretin amyloid cardiomyopathy (ATTR-CM), occurs when the liver-derived, tetrameric transport protein transthyretin (TTR) destabilizes [6]. Dissociated TTR monomers misfold and aggregate into amyloid fibrils that infiltrate the myocardium [6]. ATTR-CM is classified as either wild-type ATTR (ATTRwt), an acquired age-related condition predominantly affecting older males, or hereditary variant ATTR (ATTRv), which is caused by autosomal dominant mutations in the *TTR* gene [7,8].

### Clinical Presentation and "Red Flags"
A major historical barrier to managing CA has been delayed or missed diagnosis. Because early symptoms often mimic common hypertensive or hypertrophic cardiomyopathies, clinicians must maintain a high index of suspicion [9]. Systemic "red flags" are crucial clinical clues that should prompt immediate evaluation [9]. Non-cardiac clues include bilateral carpal tunnel syndrome, lumbar spinal stenosis, orthostatic hypotension, gastrointestinal dysmotility, and distal biceps tendon rupture [2,9]. On electrocardiography (ECG), the classic finding is low QRS voltages, which is highly suggestive when discordant with the severity of left ventricular (LV) wall thickening observed on echocardiography [10].

### Diagnostic Evaluation and Non-Invasive Pathways
Modern diagnostic frameworks emphasize multimodality imaging to secure a non-invasive diagnosis where possible, bypassing the traditional gold standard of endomyocardial biopsy [11,12]. This diagnostic paradigm relies on a validated non-biopsy algorithm that combines serum and urine screening with bone-seeking radiotracer scintigraphy [13]. Prognostic risk is stratified at baseline using staging systems based on cardiac biomarkers (e.g., N-terminal pro-B-type natriuretic peptide [NT-proBNP] and troponins) and renal function [14,15]. Regular monitoring of serum free light chains (sFLC) and cardiac biomarkers is essential to determine hematologic and organ response [16].

Transthoracic echocardiography remains the standard initial screening tool. Key structural abnormalities include concentric biventricular hypertrophy, a granular "sparkling" myocardial appearance, biatrial enlargement, and thickened valvular structures [2]. Speckle-tracking echocardiography demonstrates a highly sensitive and specific "relative apical sparing" pattern of longitudinal strain, where contractility is preserved at the apex but severely depressed at the base and mid-ventricle [17].

Cardiovascular magnetic resonance (CMR) imaging provides advanced myocardial tissue characterization. Late gadolinium enhancement (LGE) is a hallmark of CA, classically presenting as diffuse, subendocardial, or transmural enhancement with abnormal gadolinium kinetics [18]. Native T1 mapping allows non-contrast quantification of myocardial amyloid infiltration [19], while T1-derived extracellular volume (ECV) mapping quantifies the extent of the interstitial amyloid burden, serving as a powerful surrogate for disease severity and progression [20].

When AL-CA is excluded—defined by the absence of monoclonal proteins via serum/urine immunofixation and a normal sFLC ratio—bone scintigraphy using technetium-99m labeled tracers (such as ^99mTc-pyrophosphate [PYP] or ^99mTc-DPD) represents a highly sensitive and specific modality to confirm ATTR-CM [21]. Intense myocardial radiotracer retention (Grade 2 or 3 visual uptake) in the absence of a clonal plasma cell disorder is fully diagnostic of ATTR-CM, completely avoiding the need for a biopsy [13].

### Contemporary Therapeutic Management
Therapeutic management is strictly dictated by the amyloid precursor protein subtype. In AL-CA, the therapeutic mandate is to rapidly eliminate the clonal plasma cell population to halt toxic light chain production [22]. The historical standard of alkylator-based regimens, such as bortezomib, melphalan, and dexamethasone (BMDex) [23], has been revolutionized by monoclonal antibodies. The landmark phase III ANDROMEDA trial demonstrated that adding the anti-CD38 antibody daratumumab to the cyclophosphamide, bortezomib, and dexamethasone (CyBorD) backbone achieves exceptionally rapid and deep hematologic responses, translating to significantly improved organ survival [24]. For eligible patients with adequate organ reserve, high-dose chemotherapy followed by autologous stem cell transplantation (ASCT) remains a key consolidation therapy [25].

For ATTR-CM, treatment strategies focus on stabilizing the TTR tetramer or silencing its hepatic synthesis [6]. The oral TTR stabilizer tafamidis binds to the thyroxine-binding sites of TTR, preventing tetramer dissociation. In the pivotal ATTR-ACT trial, tafamidis significantly reduced all-cause mortality and cardiovascular-related hospitalizations, while slowing the decline in functional capacity and quality of life [26]. 

Alternative strategies employ gene-silencing therapeutics that degrade TTR messenger RNA to suppress TTR production. Patisiran, an intravenous small interfering RNA (siRNA) formulated in lipid nanoparticles, has demonstrated efficacy in halting neuropathy [27] and was evaluated for ATTR-CM in the APOLLO-B trial, showing benefits in functional capacity [28]. Vutrisiran, a next-generation subcutaneous siRNA administered every three months, offers potent TTR knockdown and is approved for ATTRv polyneuropathy [28]. Additionally, antisense oligonucleotides (ASOs) such as inotersen [29] and the ligand-conjugated eplontersen [30] provide alternative options to suppress hepatic TTR synthesis, offering highly targeted precision therapies for this once-untreatable disease.

### Conclusion
The clinical outlook for cardiac amyloidosis has undergone a profound transformation. What was once considered an ultra-rare, terminal disease is now highly treatable. The implementation of non-biopsy diagnostic algorithms, coupled with the development of clone-directed chemotherapy for AL-CA and TTR-targeted stabilizers and silencers for ATTR-CM, has dramatically improved survival and quality of life for these patients.
